problem: Dirichlet's theorem gives infinitely many p/q with |alpha - p/q| < 1/q^2 only for irrational alpha; for rational alpha there are only finitely many such fractions other than alpha itself.
corrected: How well can a real number be approximated by $p/q$? For irrational $\alpha$, Dirichlet gives $|\alpha - p/q| < 1/q^2$ infinitely often; Roth (1955) shows algebraic irrationals cannot do much better. Irrationality proofs (Apéry's $\zeta(3)$) are quantitative statements of this kind.

problem: Roth's theorem is about algebraic irrational alpha; as written ('algebraic alpha') it includes rationals, where p/q = alpha (as pairs (ka,kb)) gives infinitely many solutions.
corrected: \Big|\alpha-\frac pq\Big| < \frac{1}{q^{2+\varepsilon}} \ \text{has finitely many solutions for algebraic irrational } \alpha \ \text{(Roth)}
